predictions.title: HAWK enlarges its parameters rather than rebutting the attack by H1 2027
predictions.body:
Anthropic's Frontier Red Team published cryptanalysis on Tuesday, July 28 produced with Claude Mythos Preview, and the HAWK half of it lands on a standardisation process rather than on anything running in production. HAWK is a lattice-based digital signature scheme still listed as a third-round candidate in NIST's post-quantum standardisation process. The model surfaced a previously unexploited mathematical symmetry in the lattice structure that halves the effective key size, and the write-up carries numbers rather than adjectives. For the HAWK-256 challenge parameter set the work factor drops from roughly 2^64 to roughly 2^38, with an expected end-to-end runtime of about three hours and 42 minutes on a 96-core server. For the parameter sets that carry the NIST security-level claims, the gate-count estimates fall from 2^150 to 2^108 for HAWK-512 and from 2^288 to 2^182 for HAWK-1024. Nothing deployed is exposed by any of it, because HAWK is undeployed, and the result required substantial human verification after the model produced it. But gate counts are the quantity a parameter set is sized against in the first place. A 42-bit drop on HAWK-512 and a 106-bit drop on HAWK-1024 do not make the scheme attackable in the field; they make the published parameters support a weaker claim than the one they were selected to support.

The prediction is about the repair rather than the break. Through the close of H1 2027, HAWK's designers answer the symmetry with enlarged parameter sets that restore the claimed security levels — a specification revision, re-computed gate-count tables, a re-sized HAWK-512 and HAWK-1024 — and they do not answer it with a rebuttal disputing the symmetry itself. The choice between conceding and contesting is not a matter of temperament here; it is set by what the result costs an outsider to check. A 2^38 key recovery is the rare cryptanalytic claim a third party can settle outright, because settling it means renting a 96-core machine for an afternoon rather than following a chain of arguments to its end. The Hacker News noted on July 28 that it had not located an independent reproduction of the HAWK-256 key recovery. That is a real gap, and it is the kind of gap that closes on its own, because anyone motivated to close it can afford to. A rebuttal issued into that situation has about the shelf life of one cloud invoice. Enlarging parameters, by contrast, costs key and signature size and concedes nothing about whether the symmetry was found by a person or by a model.

The same publication's second result marks the boundary from the other side. An improved meet-in-the-middle attack on 7-round AES-128 — the reduced research variant, not the 10-round construction in production use — runs 200 to 800 times faster than the best previously known by removing a 256-way enumeration step, and it still needs on the order of 2^105 chosen plaintexts, so it will never be executed and can only ever be argued on paper. That result can be contested indefinitely; the HAWK one cannot. The cost line points the same way. Anthropic put the HAWK work at about a week of one researcher's time, roughly 100,000 dollars of API spend and about 60 hours inside a multi-agent environment, and the AES refinement at roughly a billion output tokens across about three days of largely autonomous work. At those prices a disputed result invites a second run rather than a correspondence, and that is precisely the condition under which a design team stops arguing and starts re-sizing.

reasoning.because: Claude Mythos Preview found a lattice symmetry cutting HAWK-512's gate count from 2^150 to 2^108
reasoning.given: A 2^38 recovery costs hours on one 96-core server, so a rebuttal cannot outlast outside checks
reasoning.so_that: HAWK's team publishes enlarged parameter sets restoring the claimed security levels instead of contesting the symmetry
reasoning.landing: by H1 2027; a HAWK team specification update or NIST-process posting
reasoning.plain_language: A model found a shortcut that weakens a proposed digital-signature system. Its designers will enlarge the keys rather than argue the shortcut is wrong.

predictions.summary: Claude Mythos Preview found a lattice symmetry halving HAWK's effective key size, cutting HAWK-512's gate count from 2^150 to 2^108 and HAWK-1024's from 2^288 to 2^182. A 2^38 HAWK-256 recovery is cheap enough to reproduce that rebuttal is untenable, so enlarged parameters follow by H1 2027.

predictions.title: FCC bars Chinese robots and inverters already cleared for sale by Q2 2027
predictions.body: The Federal Communications Commission's measures of Tuesday, July 28 reach only forward. New Chinese humanoid and quadruped robot models, and new connected power inverters, cannot obtain equipment authorisation for the US market, but models already authorised for sale stay on it and deployed units keep running; the commission noted only that it retains the power to revoke those authorisations. That line is unstable because the stated rationale does not respect it. The security case is remote commandeering and data collection by devices sitting on American networks and grid infrastructure, and the precedent the commission cites is Volt Typhoon, the 2023 campaign that worked by seizing routers people had already bought and installed. A rule written against unreleased models does not touch the population that precedent is about. What changed on the same Tuesday is the cost of closing the gap. Counterpoint Research puts Unitree at just under a fifth of global humanoid market share and names Sungrow Power Supply and the already heavily sanctioned Huawei as inverter leaders, so reaching backwards would strand a real installed base. Against that, minority shareholder Humanoid Global disclosed that Agility Robotics has a definitive business combination agreement with Churchill Capital Corp XI at a 2.5 billion dollar pre-money equity value, with closing expected during 2026 and more than 620 million dollars of gross proceeds, alongside a 60,000-square-foot Fremont physical-AI development facility, roughly 200 added technical and field-operations roles, and more than 300 million dollars of multi-year Digit v5 orders subject to contractual milestones. A funded domestic substitute is what makes retroactive action affordable, and the politics already point that way: Representative John Moolenaar welcomed the action as strengthening domestic robotics, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has warned that Chinese AI firms could face sanctions over intellectual-property theft. The prediction is that the prospective-only line does not hold. By Q2 2027 the commission takes a formal step that reaches models already authorised for US sale in the categories the July 28 measures named: revoking at least one such authorisation, or issuing a further measure that subjects the already-cleared population to the same bar. Which instrument it uses is open; that the bar reaches backwards is the claim.

reasoning.because: The July 28 FCC bar covers only unreleased models; already-authorised Chinese units stay on sale
reasoning.given: The cited Volt Typhoon precedent is about already-deployed gear, and a funded US substitute exists
reasoning.so_that: The commission revokes existing authorisations or otherwise extends the bar to models already cleared for US sale
reasoning.landing: by Q2 2027; an FCC revocation or order naming already-authorised models
reasoning.plain_language: America just blocked new Chinese robots but let the ones already approved keep selling. That gap probably closes within a year.

predictions.summary: The FCC's July 28 bar on new Chinese robots and connected inverters leaves already-authorised models on sale. That carve-out sits badly with the commission's own Volt Typhoon reasoning, and a newly funded domestic alternative lowers the cost of closing it by Q2 2027.

predictions.title: Pre-release capability testing displaces the open-weights ban debate by H1 2027
predictions.body: Anthropic published its position on open-weights models on Monday, July 27, and the opening move is a denial rather than a demand: Dario Amodei writes that Anthropic has never advocated for a ban, and that open-weights models without dangerous capabilities are a public good that costs nothing beyond the compute to run them. On Tuesday, July 28, Jensen Huang put NVIDIA on the same side of that particular question, posting that open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable national sovereignty, having already signed the open letter alongside IBM, Mozilla, Microsoft and Meta. The two do not agree about much else here — Huang says open models strengthen safety, while Amodei accepts that open weights expand access and competition but disputes that they necessarily improve safety or advantage defenders over attackers — and that is precisely why their agreement on the prohibition matters: the prohibition is no longer where the argument lives. What is left contested is the third of Anthropic's three asks, that every sufficiently capable model, open or closed and regardless of country of origin, be tested for cyber, biological and alignment risk before release. The load-bearing words are 'sufficiently capable'. That is a threshold rather than a principle, and it quietly decides which releases a gate touches, who runs the battery, and whether an origin-neutral rule can reach a foreign open-weight release at all. This prediction says that threshold becomes the contested text: by H1 2027, an explicit capability line paired with a named pre-release test for cyber, biological and alignment risk appears in at least one instrument written to bind — a federal rule or bill text, or a multi-signatory industry specification — and the open-weights side argues about where the line sits and who holds the pen rather than about whether weights may be published at all. The competing line is already on the table, which is why this should be a fight rather than a drafting exercise: the administration is weighing restrictions on Chinese AI labs, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has threatened to sanction Chinese developers of open-weight frontier models, a rule keyed to origin rather than to capability. Anthropic's own concession, that many of the companies running industrial-scale distillation operations also publish open weights, is what makes an origin-keyed or licence-keyed line messy and leaves the capability-keyed one as the residual option. The difficulty of drafting it is visible in the same week's other document: Amodei also signed the Pacing the Frontier statement published Tuesday, July 28, which says the world currently lacks the technical and governance tools to pace frontier-wide progress at all. A pre-release gate that nobody has yet specified is the narrower instance of that same missing toolkit, and specifying it is the work the next three quarters of this argument will be about.

reasoning.because: Anthropic (July 27) and NVIDIA's Jensen Huang (July 28) both rejected a blanket open-weights ban
reasoning.given: Once both camps concede the ban, the only lever left is the line deciding which models get gated
reasoning.so_that: An explicit capability threshold plus a named pre-release cyber, biological and alignment test lands in binding text
reasoning.landing: by H1 2027; threshold text in a US federal instrument or an industry spec
reasoning.plain_language: Both sides now agree open models shouldn't be banned, so the fight moves to which models must be safety-tested first.

predictions.summary: Anthropic and NVIDIA landed on the same side of the open-weights ban question within two days, which moves the argument onto the gate instead. Expect the contested text by H1 2027 to be a capability threshold plus a pre-release cyber, biological and alignment test.
